executive_summary: The market is growing fast, but no operator makes money in it — Sales grew 42% a year in 2022–25, yet both incumbents lose money on every order (p. 4, 5)

A Parcelbird store would lose money on every order, and customers don't stay long enough to repay their acquisition cost — A store loses $6.17 per order at the median; only the founders' plan, beyond any site observed, makes money — Our pop-up lost $12.57 per order, and only 22% of its customers still ordered in month 3 (p. 7–14)
Even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the investors' cash constraints — It needs $9.5M against $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; with core burn, cash runs out in month 13 (p. 16)

The software business is a better use of the same cash — It breaks even in about month 26 at today's 60% growth and month 36 at 40% — It keeps 12 months of runway as long as ARR grows 34% a year or more (p. 18–21)

Decline the launch, back software-first in phased steps, and set triggers for any return to quick commerce — The launch case meets none of its six conditions; a 90-day checkpoint gates the second tranche of hires (p. 23–26)

slides.title: The market is growing fast, but no operator makes money in it
Demand is real: US quick-commerce grocery sales grew 42% a year from 2022 to 2025

claims.claim: US quick-commerce grocery sales grew 42% a year from 2022 to 2025
evidence: US quick-commerce grocery sales (GMV), $ billions: 2022 1.8; 2023 2.6; 2024 3.6; 2025 5.1
41.5% average annual growth, 2022–25

claims.claim: Every year: growth stayed between 38% and 44% a year, with no sign of slowing in 2025
Founders' premise: the market is "growing over 40% a year"; the data bear that out
What it does not show: whether anyone earns money on these sales

slides.title: Yet none of that growth has become profit, with both incumbents losing money on every order and one already retreating

claims.claim: Both lose a quarter or more of revenue at EBITDA level
evidence: EBITDA margin, 2025: Zipcart -0.258333; QuickBasket -0.457143
Zipcart (national): $1,200M revenue, −$310M EBITDA; QuickBasket (regional): $210M revenue, −$96M EBITDA, 2025

claims.claim: Both lose money on each order before any overhead
evidence: Contribution per order, $, 2025: Zipcart -1.9; QuickBasket -3.4
Contribution per order as reported; the pack does not define it

claims.claim: QuickBasket is already pulling back
evidence: 36% of QuickBasket's cities closed in 2025 (4 of 11)

claims.claim: Zipcart is positive only in its densest city, after a fee rise (p. 14)
"Nobody owns the Midwest" may mean nobody has made it pay; growth alone does not justify entry

slides.title: Unit economics
A store at benchmark-median inputs would lose $6.17 per order, $2.67 of it before any site cost, which volume cannot fix

claims.claim: Each order brings in $11.17 but costs $13.84 before rent and staff; riders alone take 81% of the goods margin
evidence: Waterfall, benchmark median of 14 customer sites, 2025: Goods margin (27% × $34) 9.18; Delivery fee 1.99; Promotions (6% × $34) -2.04; Picking & packing -3.10; Rider ($17.75 ÷ 2.4) -6.03 to -1.36583 (bar spanning 6.03 above and 1.36583 below zero); Payment & packaging -1.3; Before site fixed cost -2.66583

claims.claim: Spreading the $1.15M a year of site cost adds $3.50 per order
evidence: Before site fixed cost -2.66583; Site fixed cost ($1.15M ÷ 900 × 365) -3.50076; After site fixed cost -6.16659

claims.claim: Higher density spreads the $3.50 of site cost thinner, but each extra order still loses $2.67; only a sharp rise in AOV or rider productivity turns it positive
Riders are the biggest cost line; two of the three plan cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers (p. 24)

slides.title: Only the founders' plan makes money; even the best-observed result on every driver at once loses $1.76 per order

claims.claim: Only the founders' plan makes money; even the best-observed result on every driver at once loses $1.76 per order
evidence: Before site fixed cost: Columbus pop-up (actual) -6.21238; Benchmark median -2.66583; Best observed (all drivers) 0.493333; Founders' plan 3.76857
After site fixed cost: Columbus pop-up -12.5725; Benchmark median -6.16659; Best observed -1.75716; Founders' plan 2.01819

claims.claim: No site has achieved even the best case
evidence: Best case: the best AOV ($42) and the best density (1,400 a day) come from different sites; combining them is already optimistic

claims.claim: Break-even AOV: with other inputs held, $63 for the median store and $50 for the best observed, against $34 and $42
Nine stores a year: −$18.2M at the median, −$8.1M at best observed, +$11.9M on the plan; only the plan's inputs give a profitable network
evidence: 9-store figures = after site cost × orders a day × 365 × 9

slides.title: The founders' plan needs results beyond the best site ever observed on all four drivers

claims.claim: The founders' plan needs results beyond the best site ever observed on all four drivers
evidence: Average order value: Observed range n/a; Median $34; Best $42; Plan $45; Plan vs best +7%
Promotions, % of AOV: Observed Pop-up: 12%; Median 6%; Best 6%; Plan 2%; −4 pp
Orders per rider-hour: 1.9–3.0; Median 2.4; Best 3; Plan 3.5; +17%, above the range
Orders per site per day: 400–1,400; Median 900; Best 1,400; Plan 1,800; +29%, above the range

claims.claim: At plan density, three mid-size cities would outsell a whole incumbent
evidence: Plan sales: 9 stores × 1,800 orders a day × $45, over a full year, = $266M in three mid-size cities
Against QuickBasket: more than its total 2025 revenue of $210M across all its cities
Against the market: about 5% of the entire 2025 US market of $5.1B

slides.title: If AOV or rider productivity only reaches the median, the founders' plan loses money again

claims.claim: If AOV or rider productivity only reaches the median, the founders' plan loses money again
evidence: Plan contribution per order after site fixed cost: Plan as proposed 2.01819; AOV $45 → $34 -0.73181; Riders 3.5 → 2.4 an hour -0.306214; Orders a day 1,800 → 900 0.26781; Promotions 2% → 6% 0.21819

claims.claim: The plan rests on the two drivers it stretches furthest
evidence: AOV and riders: at the median, either one alone turns the plan negative (−$0.73 and −$0.31 per order)

claims.claim: Density or promotions alone: a thin margin of about $0.2–0.3 per order remains, but nothing for HQ overhead or marketing
All four at the median: the plan becomes the benchmark store, at −$6.17 per order

slides.title: Our Columbus pop-up trailed the benchmark median on all four drivers, leaving no evidence of a capability edge

claims.claim: But growth was bought

slides.title: Customers don't stay: 44% say they would order weekly, but only 22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month 3

evidence: Survey of 1,500 Columbus residents
One age group only: 25–39, the core convenience segment
Says nothing about price, fees or promotions

slides.title: At that retention a customer never repays acquisition cost at median economics and takes over a year on the founders' plan

claims.claim: At that retention a customer never repays acquisition cost at median economics and takes over a year on the founders' plan
evidence: Columbus pop-up: −$6.21; Never; Never
Benchmark median: −$2.67; Never; Never

Founders' plan: +$3.77; 10 orders; 15 months

evidence: Median and pop-up: each order loses money before any site cost, so every customer acquired adds to the losses
Best observed: 77 orders to repay one customer, at 0.68 orders a month
Founders' plan: 10 orders, or 15 months, still more than a year

slides.title: Zipcart's route to profit (a $3.99 fee, 1% promotions, 14% less volume) still leaves our median store losing $1.05 per order

evidence: Benchmark median -6.16659; +$3.99 service fee +3.99; Promotions 6% → 1% +1.7; Volume −14%: site cost per order -0.569891; With Zipcart's moves -1.04649

16% above today's median and 3.7 times the pop-up, with no loss of rider productivity at the lower volume

claims.claim: Read-across: not where a new entrant starts, and nothing in our data shows it yet

slides.title: Even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the investors' cash constraints
Even on the founders' numbers the launch breaks the runway rule; with core burn added, cash runs out in month 13

claims.claim: The plan needs $9.5M; only $7.2M can be spent above the 12-month runway floor
evidence: Cash in bank 12; 12-month runway floor (12 × $0.4M) 4.8; Founders' cash need to month 18 -2.3 below zero after 7.2; Shortfall -2.3

evidence: 13: month in which cash runs out if the $9.5M comes on top of today's core burn
Runway falls below 12 months in month 5
All-in reading: $2.5M left at month 18, about 6 months of runway against 12

claims.claim: At benchmark economics 9 stores lose about $18M a year ($1.5M a month), more than our total cash
A new round for a delivery operator is "unlikely"

slides.title: The alternative
Of the three options, only software-first meets both investor constraints and keeps a foothold in fast delivery

claims.claim: A. Launch Parcelbird Now (9 dark stores, 3 cities) fails the constraints
evidence: Per-order economics: No: −$6.17 at the median; positive only on plan inputs
Cash need: No: $9.5M to month 18 (plan)
12-month runway rule: No: breached in month 5; cash out in month 13
Path to profit: No: only if every driver beats the best observed
Strategic fit: No: competes with the grocers we sell to; distracts the team
Main risk: Unit economics never close; cash runs out

claims.claim: B. One permanent pilot store (Columbus) fails the constraints
evidence: Per-order economics: No: −$6.17 at the median; −$12.57 pop-up actual
Cash need: Partly: $0.6M capex + about $2.0M a year of losses
12-month runway rule: No: breached in month 10
Path to profit: No: a single store cannot reach scale
Strategic fit: Partly: little new learning, as pop-up and 14-site data already exist
Main risk: Losses with no route to scale

claims.claim: C. Software-first + store-based fast delivery for grocers (recommended) meets both constraints
evidence: Per-order economics: Yes: 81% gross margin on $96k contracts
Cash need: Yes: $0.8M a year of hires, phased
12-month runway rule: Yes: never below about 24 months at 60% growth
Path to profit: Yes: break-even in month 26 (60% growth) or 36 (40%)
Strategic fit: Yes: meets demand already in the pipeline
Main risk: ARR growth falls below 34% a year

slides.title: Launching runs out of cash in month 13 and a pilot nears zero, while software-first bottoms at $5.4M and recovers

claims.claim: Only software-first keeps 12 months of runway throughout
evidence: Projected cash balance, $M, months 0–36, software ARR +60% a year: C. Software-first 12 at month 0, 5.39142 at month 25, 7.54418 at month 36; A. Launch 12 at month 0, -0.375271 at month 13, -2.53818 at month 22, 0.444187 at month 36; B. One pilot store 12 at month 0, 0.159568 at month 30, 0.866983 at month 36

claims.claim: A, launch: below 12 months of runway in month 5, cash out in month 13, and a low of −$2.5M in month 22
B, pilot store: below 12 months of runway in month 10, and a low of $0.2M in year 3
C, software-first: never below 12 months of runway; cash bottoms at $5.4M in month 25 and rises after break-even in month 26

slides.title: Software-first stays within current cash and the runway rule if ARR grows 34% a year or more, over half today's rate

claims.claim: 34% minimum annual ARR growth that keeps 12 months of runway
evidence: Lowest runway re-run: 12.4 months at 34% growth, 10.8 months at 33%
Cash balance months 0–48: 60% series low 5.39142 (month 25), 16.3305 at month 48; 40% series low 2.67679 (month 35), 4.75765 at month 48; 34% series low 1.24619 (month 40), 1.86337 at month 48

claims.claim: 60%, today's rate: break-even in month 26, low of $5.4M, runway never below about 24 months
40%: break-even in month 36, low of $2.7M, runway at least 18 months
34%: break-even in month 41, low of $1.2M, runway just holds at 12 months
25% (not drawn): no break-even by month 48; cash runs out and the rule is breached

slides.title: Software-first needs about 15 net new contracts in year 1 at the 34% minimum, with costs flat apart from the hires

claims.claim: Software-first needs about 15 net new contracts in year 1 at the 34% minimum
evidence: $4.1M software ARR today × 34% ÷ $96K average contract value = 14.5 net new contracts in year 1, about 15 (about 26 at today's 60%)

claims.claim: The pipeline supports the hires, but win rates are unknown, so hiring is phased
evidence: Break-even ARR = opex ÷ 81% = $8.9M ÷ 0.81 = $11.0M, against $4.1M today
The 9 late-stage grocers are worth $0.86M of ARR; all 37 in the pipeline are worth $3.55M
The $0.8M a year of hires pays for itself with about 10 contracts (28% of the pipeline)
Costs stay flat apart from the hires; the model holds opex at today's level
The pack gives no churn or win rates: release the hires in tranches against signed contracts

slides.title: Decline the launch, back software-first in phased steps, and set triggers for any return to quick commerce
Taken together, the founders' launch case needs six conditions to hold, and the evidence supports none of them

claims.claim: 1. A profit pool, not just growth: Not met
evidence: GMV +42% a year, but contribution per order is −$1.90 (Zipcart) and −$3.40 (QuickBasket); QuickBasket shut 36% of its cities

claims.claim: 2. Profit per order at achievable inputs: Not met
evidence: −$6.17 per order at the benchmark median; −$1.76 even with every best-observed input combined

claims.claim: 3. We run stores better than the benchmark: Not shown
evidence: The pop-up was below the median on all four drivers (AOV, promotions, rider productivity, density)

claims.claim: 4. Customers repay their acquisition cost: Not met
evidence: $38 CAC; 22% still ordering in month 3; CAC is never repaid at benchmark or pop-up economics

claims.claim: 5. Fits current cash with 12 months of runway: Not met
evidence: $9.5M needed against $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; no new funding expected

claims.claim: 6. Beats the best other use of the cash: Not met
evidence: The software business can reach break-even within current cash if growth stays at 34% or more

claims.claim: Every condition fails, so we reverse the hypothesis: decline the launch and invest in the software business
evidence: Initial hypothesis tested: "Launch Parcelbird Now: 9 dark stores in 3 cities, contribution-positive per order by month 18"

slides.title: The recommendation holds: most uncertainties would make a launch worse, and the risks to software-first can be managed

claims.claim: Rider minimum-pay rules (2 of 3 cities): Strengthens "don't launch"
evidence: +20% rider cost = +$1.48 per order at the median, +$1.01 on the plan

claims.claim: Density in mid-size Midwest cities: Strengthens "don't launch"
evidence: Pop-up 280 a day against a median of 900; benchmark range 400–1,400

claims.claim: Raising AOV could erode the convenience use case: Strengthens "don't launch"
evidence: The plan needs $45, against $42 best observed and $31 at the pop-up

claims.claim: A competitor claims the Midwest first: Low: first-mover status has not created profit
evidence: Incumbents are retreating (QuickBasket closed 4 cities) and lose money per order

claims.claim: Software growth slows below the minimum: Main risk to C
evidence: Below 34% a year, C breaches the runway rule; at 25% it runs out of cash

claims.claim: Software cost base grows faster than assumed: Delays C's break-even
evidence: The model holds opex flat apart from the $0.8M of hires

claims.claim: Grocers' own fast delivery competes with our customers: Upside for C
evidence: Several pipeline grocers want store-based fast delivery

slides.title: We would reconsider an operator model only when customer sites prove the economics and dedicated funding exists

claims.claim: 1. Site-level profit is proven: At least one customer site shows positive contribution after site cost for two consecutive quarters
evidence: Today: none
Best-observed inputs give −$1.76 per order

claims.claim: 2. The profit drivers are seen at one site at the same time: AOV of $42 or more and 3.0 or more orders per rider-hour at 1,050 or more orders a day, or a service fee that does the same job without losing more than 15% of volume
evidence: Today: no site has both
Break-even with Zipcart's moves needs about 1,042 orders a day

claims.claim: 3. Customers stay: Month-3 retention high enough to repay $38 of acquisition cost within 12 months at actual contribution
evidence: Today: 22% at 3.1 orders a month
Payback never happens at the median

claims.claim: 4. Funding is ring-fenced: Dedicated capital that leaves the core business with 12 months of runway at all times
evidence: Today: a new round is "unlikely"
Headroom is $7.2M against a $9.5M plan

slides.title: We ask the board for four decisions in January 2027 and a progress review in April

claims.claim: 1. Decline the 2027 launch of Parcelbird Now (Board, Jan 2027)
evidence: Do not commit capex to dark stores and do not extend the pop-up (annualised loss about $1.3M). Keep the pop-up data and cohort learning

claims.claim: 3. Build a store-based fast-delivery offer (CTO / Sales, Q2 2027)
evidence: Package picking and rider dispatch for grocers who want fast delivery from existing stores; test it with late-stage pipeline accounts

claims.claim: 4. Adopt re-entry triggers and runway reporting (CFO, Q1 2027)
evidence: Quarterly dashboard of the 4 triggers from customer-site data, plus monthly runway against the 12-month rule

claims.claim: At the 90-day checkpoint in April 2027, hold the second tranche of hires if ARR growth is tracking below the 34% minimum
evidence: 90-day checkpoint (April 2027): late-stage conversions against the 9 grocers, pilot interest in store-based fast delivery, actual ARR growth against the 34% minimum, and the first trigger dashboard

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Decline the launch, back software-first in phased steps, and set triggers for any return to quick commerce. Four board decisions: 1. Decline the 2027 launch of Parcelbird Now (do not commit capex to dark stores and do not extend the pop-up); 2. Approve the software scale-up (2 engineers and 2 sales hires, $0.8M a year, released in two tranches tied to signed late-stage contracts); 3. Build a store-based fast-delivery offer; 4. Adopt re-entry triggers and runway reporting. At the 90-day checkpoint in April 2027, hold the second tranche of hires if ARR growth is tracking below the 34% minimum.

alternatives_considered.option: A. Launch Parcelbird Now (9 dark stores, 3 cities)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: −$6.17 per order at the median, positive only on plan inputs; $9.5M to month 18; runway rule breached in month 5, cash out in month 13; path to profit only if every driver beats the best observed; competes with the grocers we sell to and distracts the team. Main risk: unit economics never close; cash runs out. Launch case meets none of its six conditions.

Rejected: −$6.17 at the median, −$12.57 pop-up actual; $0.6M capex + about $2.0M a year of losses; runway rule breached in month 10; a single store cannot reach scale; little new learning, as pop-up and 14-site data already exist. Main risk: losses with no route to scale. Option not in the pack; defined by the analysis.

alternatives_considered.option: C. Software-first + store-based fast delivery for grocers
alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended: 81% gross margin on $96k contracts; $0.8M a year of hires, phased; never below about 24 months of runway at 60% growth; break-even in month 26 (60% growth) or 36 (40%); meets demand already in the pipeline. Main risk: ARR growth falls below 34% a year.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Briefing pack figures are synthetic benchmark data; prepared from the board briefing pack only, no external research
Contribution per order as reported for incumbents; the pack does not define it — shown both before and after site fixed cost
Contribution excludes HQ overhead, capex and marketing
Best case combines best AOV ($42) and best density (1,400 a day) from different sites; combining them is already optimistic
The pack gives no range for AOV; promotions have no benchmark range, only the pop-up's 12%
Plan sales compare our GMV with QuickBasket's reported revenue, taken to be roughly equivalent for an operator that sells the goods itself
Pop-up week 1 and week 6 volumes are an estimate, assuming 18% weekly growth compounded evenly over six weeks
Survey and pop-up cohort are different groups; survey covers one age group only (25–39) and says nothing about price, fees or promotions
Payback calculation is generous: assumes no churn after month 3 and uses contribution before any site cost
Zipcart's volume loss applied to site cost only; assumes no loss of rider productivity at the lower volume
The pack does not say whether the $9.5M includes core burn; both readings are shown
The runway floor rises once stores are operating; the $7.2M of headroom is therefore a ceiling
Runway = cash ÷ recurring monthly burn; one-off capex excluded from the burn (lenient)

Cash model: opex held flat apart from the $0.8M a year of hires (in B and C, not in A); ARR compounds monthly; A assumes $5.4M capex at one store a month (months 1–9) plus $4.1M evenly over months 1–18, nothing after (the founders' best case)
Software opex derived as 81% × ARR + burn, since the pack gives burn not opex; optimistic for C
Contracts are net of churn, which the pack does not give; gross wins would need to be higher; the pack gives no churn or win rates
The +20% rider-cost rise is a sensitivity chosen by the analysis; the pack does not size the proposed rules
Main risk to C: software growth below 34% a year breaches the runway rule; at 25% it runs out of cash
Software cost base could grow faster than assumed, delaying C's break-even
A new round for a delivery operator is "unlikely"
Re-entry thresholds set by the analysis: 1,050 orders a day rounds up the 1,042 break-even; the 15% volume limit sits just above Zipcart's 14% loss
next_steps: Record the decision to decline the 2027 launch and close the pop-up; keep its data and cohort learning (Board, Jan 2027)
Release the first tranche of software hires against signed late-stage contracts (9 grocers, $0.86M ARR) (CEO, Q1 2027)
Stand up the quarterly re-entry trigger dashboard and monthly runway report against the 12-month rule (CFO, Q1 2027)
Test a store-based fast-delivery offer with late-stage pipeline accounts (CTO / Sales, Q2 2027)
